q: 1. An old worn out tyre may offer more friction on a dry surface than a new tyre with treads because .............
options: old surface got more accustomed for the surface of road
new tyre had a smooth surface
old surface had more contact area
hollows of treads of tyre had more friction
explain: On dry surfaces, a smooth (worn out) tyre provides a larger contact area with the pavement, resulting in higher friction compared to a treaded tyre.

q: 2. Weight of a vehicle affects the design of .............
options: camber and gradient of a road
pavement thickness and gradient of a road
explain: Pavement thickness is directly designed based on the anticipated axle loads (weight) and the number of repetitions.

q: 3. The layer that is directly coming in contact with the traffic is .............
explain: The wearing course (or surface course) is the topmost layer that resists the abrasion from traffic and provides a smooth riding surface.

q: 4. A pavement is classified as flexible pavement or rigid pavement based on its .............
explain: The distinction is primarily based on the structural action and the material of the top layer (Bituminous for flexible, Concrete for rigid).

q: 5. The first artificial course provided on a highway .............
explain: The sub-grade is natural soil; the sub-base is the first layer of man-made material placed over it to distribute loads.

q: 6. Greater unevenness causes .............
explain: High unevenness indices lead to loss of vehicle control, increased fatigue, and vehicle damage, significantly increasing accident risk.

q: 7. A pavement that offers poor visibility is .............
explain: Bituminous (black-top) roads absorb more light, leading to poor visibility at night compared to lighter-colored concrete or gravel roads.

q: 8. Seal coat is a layer of .............
options: adhesive to improve bond between aggregates
explain: A seal coat usually consists of a thin application of binder and fine aggregate (coarse sand) to seal the surface.

q: 9. Purpose of the seal coat is to provide .............
explain: The main function of a seal coat is to make the pavement surface impervious to water, preventing it from reaching the base layers.

q: 10. The best road suited to pneumatic and iron wheeled traffic is .............
explain: Cement concrete (rigid) roads are the most durable and can withstand the high abrasive stress caused by iron-wheeled carts without deforming.

q: 11. Cement concrete road can be laid over .............
options: an earthen road subjected to traffic for 1 year
a WBM road of thickness greater than 150 mm and subjected to traffic for 1 month
any black top road is use at least for 2 weeks
explain: A stable WBM base that has been compacted by traffic for at least a month provides a reliable foundation for a concrete slab.

q: 12. In water bound macadam roads, binding material, is .............
explain: WBM roads use stone screenings and stone dust, which—when mixed with water—act as a binder to fill the voids between larger aggregates.

q: 13. An ideal pavement is constructed with
explain: Portland Cement Concrete (PCC) is considered ideal for high-durability, long-life pavements with low tractive resistance.

q: 14. For maximum strength and durability minimum percentage of cement, by weight is
explain: Standard mixes like 1:2:4 or M20 roughly result in a cement content around 15% by weight of the total mix.

q: 15. To indicate proper control of consistency of a freshly mixed concrete for pavement construction, the slump should be between
explain: Road concrete requires a very stiff mix (low workability) to ensure high strength and prevent flow; hence a low slump of 3-5 cm is used.

q: 16. The formula for calculating the depth of concrete pavements suggested by Goldbeck, is
explain: Goldbeck's formula for corner loading is d = √(3W/σ), where W is the wheel load and σ is the allowable stress.

q: 17. When load is applied on concrete pavement
options: away from edges, the maximum bending moment is negative
away from edges, the maximum bending moment cause compression
on the edges, the maximum stress is parallel to the edge
explain: Interior loading (away from edges) causes the slab to deflect like a dish, creating negative bending moments and tension at the bottom.

q: 18. For the design of cement concrete pavement for corner loading, Indian Road Congress recommends the use of
explain: While Westergaard is more theoretically complex, IRC historically used simplified versions like Goldbeck's for practical corner design.

q: 19. Reinforcement in cement concrete slab of road pavements, is placed
options: in the form of welded wire mesh
explain: Reinforcement is provided in both directions to control temperature cracks and distribute loads efficiently.

q: 20. Depth of reinforcement below the surface of a concrete pavement, is generally kept
explain: A standard cover of 5 cm is maintained to protect the steel from corrosion while remaining effective in resisting surface-level stresses.

q: 21. To prevent compressive stresses in a rigid concrete pavement, the joint provided, is
explain: Expansion joints allow the slab to lengthen during hot weather, preventing compressive buckling.

q: 22. Transverse joints are provided at distances varying from
explain: Modern spacing for expansion joints in rigid pavements typically falls in the 17m to 27m range, depending on temperature variation.

q: 23. Bottom-most component of a flexible pavement, is
explain: The subgrade is the prepared natural soil foundation upon which all other layers are built.

q: 24. Thickness of a pavement may be reduced considerably by
options: combination of all of the above
explain: Improving the strength of the subgrade through any of these methods allows for a thinner (and cheaper) upper pavement structure.

q: 25. Minimum thickness of the base of a flexible pavement is
explain: A standard minimum of 10 cm is required for the base layer to ensure proper load distribution and construction stability.

q: 26. For a poorly graded sub-grade soil, thickness of sub-base, is
explain: Poorly graded soils have low bearing capacity, requiring a thick sub-base layer (30 cm) to protect the subgrade.

q: 27. The weight of vehicles affects
explain: Pavement thickness is structurally designed based on the magnitude of wheel loads and axle weights to prevent fatigue and rutting.

q: 28. The distance travelled by revolving the wheel of a vehicle more than its circumferential movement, is known as
explain: Slip occurs when the wheel rotates more than the actual distance covered (common during acceleration on slippery surfaces).

q: 29. Longitudinal pavement lines marked broken in white paint
options: are for the guidance of the drivers
are not to be crossed over
may be crossed over at the discretion of the driver
explain: Broken white lines indicate that lane changing or overtaking is permitted when safe; solid lines indicate crossing is prohibited.

q: 30. The foundation of a road is also called ............
explain: In older terminology, the foundation layer providing structural strength is often referred to as soling or the base course.

q: 31. The super structure of a road is called ............
explain: The uppermost layer in direct contact with traffic is the 'super structure,' commonly called the wearing course or road surfacing.

q: 32. The thickness of base, in no case, should be more than ............
explain: For efficient compaction and structural performance, individual base course layers are typically limited to a maximum thickness of 20 cm.

q: 33. The road surfacing should be ............
explain: To protect the lower layers and handle traffic, the surface must resist water penetration (impervious), withstand wear (durable), and maintain its shape under load (stable).

q: 34. The structure of a road is composed of ............
explain: A standard pavement structure includes the sub-grade (foundation), sub-base, base, and the surface wearing course.

q: 35. The wearing course in the case of flexible pavements consist of ............
options: broken stone and granular material mixed with tar
a mixture of bituminous material and aggregate
explain: For modern flexible pavements, the wearing course is typically a mix of aggregate and a bituminous binder (asphalt).

q: 36. The California bearing ratio (C.B.R.) method of flexible pavement design gives an idea about ............
options: the quality of road making material
explain: CBR is an empirical test that relates soil strength/stiffness to pavement thickness required for specific traffic levels.

q: 37. In C.B.R. test, the value of C.B.R. is calculated at ............
explain: CBR values are determined for both 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm penetration, and the higher value is usually reported.

q: 38. Which of the following method is recommended by I.R.C. for design of flexible pavement?
explain: The Indian Roads Congress (IRC:37) adopts the CBR method for the design of flexible pavements.

q: 39. The minimum thickness of the base of a flexible pavement is kept as ............
explain: A minimum of 10 cm is generally required for the base course to ensure proper load distribution and construction stability.

q: 40. The main advantage of concrete pavements is that ............
options: it offers less resistance to traffic
it is not slippery when clean
explain: Rigid (concrete) pavements are durable, provide a smooth riding surface, and require significantly less maintenance over their long lifespan compared to flexible ones.

q: 41. The depth of reinforcement, below the surface of pavement, is kept as ............
explain: A standard clear cover of 50 mm is typically provided for reinforcement in concrete pavements to protect the steel from corrosion and surface wear.

q: 42. Of all the forces stressing a concrete pavement, the most significant are those imposed by the ............
explain: While temperature causes warping, the primary structural design of concrete pavement is governed by the heavy concentrated wheel loads of vehicles.

q: 43. A large difference of temperature between the top and the bottom of the slab causes ............ of the slab.
explain: Temperature gradients cause the top and bottom of the slab to expand or contract at different rates, leading to 'warping' or curling of the slab edges.

q: 44. When the exposed surface of a pavement dries and shrinks more than the underlying concrete, a phenomenon known as ............ of the surface may occur.
explain: Crazing refers to a network of fine hairline cracks on the surface caused by rapid drying and shrinkage of the top layer of concrete.

q: 45. The joints, parallel to the centre-line of the road, are called ............
explain: Longitudinal joints run in the direction of traffic (parallel to the centerline) to control longitudinal cracking and delineate lanes.

q: 46. The longitudinal joints are provided when the width of road is more than ............
explain: For pavements wider than approximately 4 meters, longitudinal joints are necessary to prevent irregular longitudinal cracks caused by subgrade movement or warping.

q: 47. Longitudinal joints in concrete pavements ............
options: take care of the unequal settlement of the sub-grade
help in laying out concrete in convenient widths
explain: Longitudinal joints serve functional purposes for traffic (lanes), structural safety (settlement), and construction efficiency.

q: 48. The transverse joint may be a ............
explain: Transverse joints run perpendicular to the road centerline and include joints designed for expansion, contraction, or warping.

q: 49. The maximum spacing of contraction joints in unreinforced concrete slabs for a slab thickness of 20 cm is ............
explain: To prevent random cracking due to shrinkage, unreinforced slabs require closely spaced contraction joints, typically 4.5 m apart for standard thicknesses.

q: 50. Weight of a vehicle affects ............
explain: Heavier vehicle loads exert higher stresses on the road, which directly determines the required thickness and strength of the pavement layers.
